desc:
A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes in which every two neighbours in the sequence are parent and child, and no node is used twice. A path may start and end at any nodes and may turn at a node (go up to a common ancestor and then down again). It must contain at least one node.

Return the largest sum of node values over all paths that contain at most k nodes. Values can be negative, and the tree is guaranteed to have at least one node.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). Node values can be negative in this problem, so a missing child is written as 1000 (real node values always lie between -500 and 500, so the marker can never be confused with a value). The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing 1000 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with 1000. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, 1000, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [-10, 9, 20, 1000, 1000, 15, 7]: with k = 1 the answer is 20, with k = 2 it is 35 (15 → 20) and with k = 3 it is 42 (15 → 20 → 7).
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, missing child written as 1000, no trailing 1000)
hints: If k were unlimited this is the classic maximum path sum. The limit on the number of nodes means a single number per node is no longer enough.

For each node v and each length j up to k, store the best sum of a downward chain starting at v with at most j nodes (or 0 for taking nothing). A chain is v plus a chain of at most j - 1 nodes from one child.

A path peaking at v uses a nodes on the left and k - 1 - a on the right. Because the stored values never decrease with the allowed length, trying every a from 0 to k - 1 with the total fixed at k - 1 covers all splits with at most k - 1 nodes below v. That is O(k) per node.
editorial: Classify paths by their highest node v, as in the unrestricted problem. A path peaking at v consists of v, a downward chain of a nodes below the left child and a downward chain of b nodes below the right child, with a + b + 1 ≤ k. Now the best chain depends on its allowed length, so we keep a table.

Let c[v][j] be the best sum of a downward chain that starts at v and has at most j nodes, or 0 if taking nothing is better (so c[v][0] = 0, and a missing child is the all-zero row). Then c[v][j] = max(0, val[v] + max(c[left][j-1], c[right][j-1])). Rows are non-decreasing in j.

The best path peaking at v with at most k nodes is val[v] + max over a in [0, k-1] of (c[left][a] + c[right][k-1-a]). Because the rows never decrease, giving the two sides a total budget of exactly k - 1 already includes every split that uses fewer nodes. The answer is the maximum over all nodes (initialise it to a very small number, since every value may be negative).
Each node costs O(k) for the combination and O(k) for building its row, so the time is O(n · k). Rows of finished children can be discarded to keep memory at the size of the active frontier.
